description: Organizing content with lists and tables — bulleted, numbered, and grid-shaped.

screens.body:
An unordered list <ul> wraps list items <li> — and the browser adds the bullets for you.

<ul> means "order doesn't matter": shopping lists, feature lists, nav menus. Change your mind later? Swap <ul> for <ol> and the same items become numbered.

Only <li> goes directly inside <ul>. Nesting a <ul> inside an <li> makes sub-lists — great for menus with sub-menus.

options: A shopping list — order doesn't matter
check.question: Which list should be a <ul>?

screens.heading: Unordered lists: bullets

screens.body:
An ordered list <ol> numbers its items automatically: 1, 2, 3…

Use it when sequence matters: instructions, rankings, steps. Add a fourth <li> later and the browser renumbers everything — no manual fixing.

The start attribute changes the first number (<ol start="5"> begins at 5), and reversed counts down. The browser handles the math.

options: <ul> and type the numbers by hand
tags with numbers in the text
check.question: Which is best for a 5-step signup guide?

code.snippet:
1. Create your account
  2. Post your task
  3. Pick a helper
  4. Pay when it's done

screens.heading: Ordered lists: numbers
screens.keyPoint: <ol> + <li> = numbered list. The browser handles numbering and renumbering.

screens.body:
Tables are for data that belongs in rows and columns: schedules, price lists, stats. The structure: <table> wraps rows <tr>, and each row holds cells <td>.

Think spreadsheet: <tr> is a horizontal row, <td> is one box in that row. Every row should have the same number of cells.

Never use tables to lay out a whole page — that's a 2005 habit. CSS handles layout; tables handle data.

check.question: In a table, which tag makes a ROW?

screens.heading: Tables: rows and cells
screens.keyPoint: <table> → <tr> rows → <td> cells. Tables are for data, never page layout.

screens.body:
Header cells use <th> instead of <td> — usually the first row (column names) or first column (row names). Browsers bold and center them by default.

Add scope="col" or scope="row" so screen readers announce which header belongs to which cell: <th scope="col">Name</th>.

Without headers, a data table is just a grid of mystery numbers. With them, everyone — including screen-reader users — knows what each column means.

check.question: Which is the correct table header cell?

screens.heading: Table headers
screens.keyPoint: <th> = header cell. scope="col"/"row" tells screen readers what it labels.

screens.body:
Big tables get three sections: <thead> (headers), <tbody> (the data), <tfoot> (totals or footnotes). They must appear in that order.

This isn't just tidiness — browsers can repeat <thead> on printed pages, and screen readers use the sections to orient users in long tables.

Also give the table a <caption> as its very first child: it's the table's title, announced before the data. Like a figure caption, but for tables.

check.question: Which gives a table an announced title?

code.snippet:
October gig earnings
GigPay
Dog walking$25

screens.heading: thead, tbody, and captions
screens.keyPoint: <thead>/<tbody>/<tfoot> section big tables; <caption> is the table's title.

screens.body:
Need name-value pairs — like a glossary or FAQ? That's a description list: <dl> wraps terms <dt> and their descriptions <dd>.

One term can have several descriptions, and the browser indents descriptions for you.

It's the semantic choice for FAQs, dictionaries, and metadata ("Founded: 2026") — better than bold paragraphs pretending to be a list.

check.question: Best markup for a glossary of terms?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: description lists -->
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The markup language of the web.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The styling language of the web.</dd>
</dl>

screens.heading: Description lists

screens.body:
Cells can span multiple columns or rows: colspan="2" makes a cell stretch across two columns; rowspan="2" stretches down two rows.

Handy for grouped headers ("Q1" over Jan/Feb/Mar columns) or a total row label. Just keep the total cell count per row consistent or the table wobbles.

If your spanning gets complicated enough to need a diagram, that's a sign to simplify the table — or split it into two.

check.question: How do you make a cell span two columns?

screens.heading: Spanning cells
screens.keyPoint: colspan stretches across columns; rowspan stretches down rows.
